title: Number Sets & Intervals
blurb: The nested family ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ with the irrationals in the gap, interval notation and integer counts, intersections and unions on the number line, and absolute value read as distance — the language every inequality answer is written in.
buildsOn: Set operations and counting from Units 1–2.

lessons.title: ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ — the Nested Family
lessons.concreteComparison: Russian dolls: the naturals sit inside the integers, the integers inside the rationals, the rationals inside the reals — and the irrationals are the gap between the last two dolls.
lessons.objective: Classify numbers into $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$, recognizing disguised members and the irrationals in the gap.
concept: $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ adds zero and negatives, $\mathbb{Q}$ is all ratios $p/q$ with $q \ne 0$ — equivalently the decimals that terminate or repeat — and $\mathbb{R}$ fills the line. Each is a subset of the next.

The **irrationals** are $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$: decimals that never terminate or repeat, like $\sqrt{2}$ and $\pi$. They are a set DIFFERENCE, not a fifth doll — a number is rational or irrational, never both.
Exam classification items hide members in disguise: $\sqrt{49} = 7$ is a natural number, $\frac{18}{6} = 3$ is an integer, $0.75 = \frac{3}{4}$ is rational. Simplify FIRST, classify second.
lessons.keyIdea: $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$; irrational = real but not rational. Simplify before classifying.

facts.title: The chain
facts.explanation: Every natural is an integer, every integer rational, every rational real.

facts.title: Rational means
facts.explanation: Two equivalent tests — use whichever the number's costume invites.

workedExamples.solution: $\sqrt{49} = 7 \in \mathbb{N}$. $-\frac{12}{4} = -3 \in \mathbb{Z}$ (not $\mathbb{N}$). $0.\overline{3} = \frac{1}{3} \in \mathbb{Q}$. $\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$ is irrational — $8$ is not a perfect square.
Simplify before judging: $\frac{\sqrt{50}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ — a natural number. Irrational pieces can combine into rational results.

commonMistakes.text: Classifying $\sqrt{49}$ as irrational because it has a root sign.
commonMistakes.correction: Simplify first: $\sqrt{49} = 7$. The costume is not the number.
$\frac{22}{7}$ is an approximation, not an equality — $\pi$ has no exact fraction form, which is the definition of irrational.

tryIt.solution: $\sqrt{36} = 6$ ✓, $-\frac{20}{5} = -4$ ✓, $0.\overline{12} = \frac{12}{99} = \frac{4}{33}$ ✓; $\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. Three of the four.

tryIt.statement: Give the value of $\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{32}$ and classify it.
tryIt.solution: $\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{32} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ — a natural number, from two irrational factors.

steps.title: Four nested sets, one gap
steps.body: $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$ — each doll fits in the next. The irrationals are not a doll: they are the space between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$, defined by NOT being rational.

steps.title: Costume check
steps.explanation: $\sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt{3}$ — $12$ is not a perfect square. The others simplify to $\frac{4}{5}$, $\frac{7}{9}$ and $-5$: all rational.

steps.title: What sticks
points: Rational $\iff$ terminating or repeating decimal $\iff$ a fraction
SIMPLIFY first — roots and fractions love disguises

lessons.title: Intervals & Their Notation
lessons.concreteComparison: A bus route with stations: square bracket means the bus stops AT the station, round bracket means it passes without stopping. The route between is served either way.
lessons.objective: Convert between inequalities, number-line pictures and interval notation, including rays to infinity.
concept: $[a, b]$ includes both endpoints ($a \le x \le b$); $(a, b)$ excludes both ($a < x < b$); $[a, b)$ and $(a, b]$ mix. Square bracket = endpoint in, round = out. On a number line: filled dot vs open dot.

Rays use $\infty$: $x > 3$ is $(3, \infty)$ and $x \le -1$ is $(-\infty, -1]$. Infinity ALWAYS takes a round bracket — it is a direction, not a reachable endpoint. The whole line is $(-\infty, \infty) = \mathbb{R}$.

The length of a bounded interval is $b - a$ regardless of brackets — endpoints have zero width. But element COUNTS over the integers do depend on brackets, which is where interval work reconnects with Unit 1's counting.
lessons.keyIdea: Square bracket = endpoint included, round = excluded; $\infty$ is always round. Length $= b - a$ either way.

facts.title: The four bounded shapes
facts.explanation: Brackets record endpoint membership; the interior is the same.

facts.title: Rays
facts.explanation: Infinity is a direction — never bracketed square.

workedExamples.statement: Write $-3 < x \le 7$ in interval notation and give the interval's length.
How many INTEGERS lie in $(-3, 7]$, and how many in $[-3, 7]$?
workedExamples.solution: $(-3, 7]$ holds $-2, \ldots, 7$: that is $7 - (-2) + 1 = 10$ integers. Closing the left end adds $-3$ itself: $11$.

commonMistakes.correction: No number equals $\infty$, so it can never be 'included': $[3, \infty)$.
Both have length $3$ — single points carry no width. Only integer COUNTS change with the brackets.

tryIt.statement: Write $\{x : x \ge -4\}$ and $\{x : x < 6\}$ in interval notation, and give the length of their intersection.
How many integers are in the interval $[-5, 5)$?

steps.title: Stops and pass-throughs
steps.body: One convention carries the whole lesson: square bracket stops at the endpoint, round bracket passes it by. Translate the inequality's $\le$ vs $<$ into brackets and the notation writes itself.

steps.title: Direction, not destination
steps.prompt: Which is the correct notation for $x \le 4$?
steps.explanation: Ray to the left, endpoint included: $(-\infty, 4]$. Infinity is always round, and $4$ takes the square bracket because of $\le$.

steps.title: What sticks
points: Integer counts DO care about brackets — recount the endpoints

lessons.title: Intersections & Unions of Intervals
lessons.concreteComparison: Two friends' free time: you can meet only when BOTH are free — the later start and the earlier end. Availability of at least one of them is the union, and it may come in two separate pieces.
lessons.objective: Intersect and unite intervals on the number line, recognizing when a union stays in two pieces and when an intersection is empty.
concept: **Intersection**: keep the overlap — the interval from the LARGER left endpoint to the SMALLER right endpoint: $[a, b] \cap [c, d] = [\max(a,c), \min(b,d)]$, empty when $\max(a,c) > \min(b,d)$.

**Union**: merge when the intervals touch or overlap; otherwise the union stays as two disjoint pieces written with $\cup$. There is no simpler form of $(-\infty, 1) \cup (3, \infty)$ — leaving it in pieces IS the answer.

Systems of inequalities are interval intersections: $x > -2$ AND $x \le 5$ is $(-2, 5]$. 'Or' conditions are unions. Sketching the number line before writing notation prevents nearly every error in this lesson.
lessons.keyIdea: Intersection: $[\max(a,c), \min(b,d)]$, possibly empty. Union: merge if touching, else two pieces with $\cup$.

facts.title: Interval intersection
facts.explanation: Later start, earlier end — empty if they cross.

facts.title: And vs or
facts.explanation: The same translation as Unit 1, now on the number line.

workedExamples.solution: Later start: $\max(-4, 1) = 1$ (open, from the round bracket); earlier end: $\min(6, 9) = 6$ (closed). Intersection $(1, 6]$, length $6 - 1 = 5$.

workedExamples.statement: Solve the system $x \ge -1$ and $x < 4$ and $x \ne 2$, in interval notation.
workedExamples.solution: The first two give $[-1, 4)$; removing the single point $2$ splits it: $[-1, 2) \cup (2, 4)$. Lengths $2 - (-1) = 3$ and $4 - 2 = 2$ — total $5$, the original length, since a point has no width.

commonMistakes.text: Merging a two-piece union into one interval: $(-\infty,1) \cup (3,\infty) = (3,1)$?
commonMistakes.correction: If the pieces do not touch, they stay separate. $(3, 1)$ is not even an interval — the union keeps its $\cup$.

commonMistakes.text: Taking the smaller left endpoint for an intersection.
commonMistakes.correction: Intersection starts where BOTH have started: the LARGER left endpoint. The smaller one belongs to the union.

tryIt.statement: Find $(-\infty, 3] \cap (-2, \infty)$ and the number of integers in it.
tryIt.solution: Overlap: $(-2, 3]$, holding integers $-1, 0, 1, 2, 3$ — that is $3 - (-1) + 1 = 5$ of them.

tryIt.statement: Is $[5, 8] \cap [9, 12]$ empty? Justify with the endpoint rule.
tryIt.solution: $\max(5, 9) = 9 > \min(8, 12) = 8$ — the later start comes after the earlier end, so the intersection is $\varnothing$.

steps.title: Later start, earlier end
steps.body: Every interval intersection is the same two comparisons: the overlap begins at the larger left endpoint and ends at the smaller right one. If those cross, there is no overlap at all.

steps.title: Sketch first
steps.explanation: The pieces meet exactly at $2$, which the right piece includes — together they tile the whole line: $\mathbb{R}$.

steps.title: What sticks
points: Unions merge only when the pieces touch; otherwise keep the $\cup$
Sketch the line first — notation second

lessons.title: Absolute Value as Distance
lessons.concreteComparison: A leash staked at point $a$: $|x - a| < r$ is everywhere the dog can reach — the open interval of radius $r$ around the stake. Cut the leash ($> r$) and the dog is anywhere OUTSIDE that stretch.
lessons.objective: Translate $|x - a| < r$ and $|x - a| > r$ into intervals and unions of rays, and write a given interval as an absolute-value condition.
concept: $|x - a|$ is the DISTANCE from $x$ to $a$. So $|x - a| < r$ collects the points within $r$ of $a$: the interval $(a - r, a + r)$. With $\le$ the endpoints join: $[a - r, a + r]$.
$|x - a| > r$ is the far side of the leash: $(-\infty, a - r) \cup (a + r, \infty)$ — always TWO pieces. An absolute-value 'greater than' never collapses to a single interval.

Backwards is the exam's favorite: the interval $(2, 10)$ has center $\frac{2 + 10}{2} = 6$ and radius $\frac{10 - 2}{2} = 4$, so it is exactly $|x - 6| < 4$. Center–radius form makes any symmetric condition one line.
lessons.keyIdea: $|x - a| < r \iff a - r < x < a + r$; the $>$ version is the two-ray outside. Interval $\to$ condition via center and radius.

facts.title: Within the leash
facts.latex: |x - a| < r \iff x \in (a - r,\ a + r)
facts.explanation: Distance below $r$: the open ball around $a$.

facts.title: Center and radius
facts.explanation: Any interval $(p, q)$ is $|x - a| < r$ with these values.

workedExamples.statement: Solve $|x - 3| \le 5$ and count the integers in the solution set.
Write the interval $(-1, 9)$ as an absolute-value inequality.

commonMistakes.correction: 'Greater than' is the OUTSIDE: $(-\infty, -2) \cup (8, \infty)$. The single interval is the $<$ case.
$|x + 2| = |x - (-2)|$ — the center is $-2$. Rewrite the inside as $x - a$ before reading off the center.

tryIt.statement: Write $[1, 13]$ in the form $|x - a| \le r$.

steps.title: Distance, pictured
steps.body: Read $|x - a|$ as 'how far $x$ is from $a$' and both inequality types become geometry: $< r$ is the stretch within reach, $> r$ is everything beyond it — two rays, always.

steps.title: Inside or outside
steps.explanation: Distance from $6$ exceeding $2$ puts $x$ beyond $4$ on the left or beyond $8$ on the right — both rays, not just one.

steps.title: The ε you will meet again
steps.body: University analysis defines limits with exactly this lesson: $|x - a| < \varepsilon$ as 'within $\varepsilon$ of $a$'. The leash picture you built here is the mental model for all of calculus's rigor.

steps.title: What sticks
points: $|x - a| < r$: interval $(a - r, a + r)$; $\le$ closes it
$|x - a| > r$: two rays — never one interval

practice.statement: Classify $\sqrt{81}$, $-\frac{14}{2}$, $\sqrt{20}$, $0.\overline{45}$ as natural, integer, rational or irrational (most specific set).
Write $-6 \le x < 2$ in interval notation; give its length and the number of integers it contains.

practice.solution: Intersection: $[\max(-2,0), \min(5,8))$ with the appropriate brackets $= [0, 5)$. The pieces overlap, so the union merges: $[-2, 8]$.

practice.statement: Solve $|x - 5| < 3$ and state how many integers satisfy it.
Write the set $\{x : 3 < x < 11\}$ as an absolute-value inequality.
Solve the system $x > -3$, $x \le 6$, $x \ne 0$ in interval notation.
For which integer values of $x$ is $|x - 4| \le 2$ AND $x$ even?
practice.solution: $[2, 6]$ holds integers $2,3,4,5,6$; the even ones are $2, 4, 6$ — three values.

practice.statement: The intervals $[a, 10]$ and $[4, 7]$ intersect in a set of length $3$. If $a \le 4$, find the intersection.
practice.solution: With $a \le 4$ the overlap is $[\max(a,4), \min(10,7)] = [4, 7]$ — length $7 - 4 = 3$ ✓, so the intersection is $[4, 7]$ itself.

testYourself.solution: $\sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}$ — the only irrational; $\sqrt{64} = 8$, and the other two are fractions by form ($0.1\overline{6} = \frac{1}{6}$).
Overlap from the later start $-1$ (closed) to the earlier end $4$ (open): $[-1, 4)$.

testYourself.statement: Write $[-9, 1]$ in the form $|x - a| \le r$.
How many integers satisfy $|x| < 6$ but NOT $|x| < 2$?
